messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Omar was a 40-year-old married paramedic who had always prided himself on staying composed when other people were panicking. The trauma that unsettled that confidence was not something that happened to him, but something he witnessed up close: during a late-night call, he arrived to find a young victim with severe visible injuries, blood already soaking through clothing, the corridor around the stretcher carrying that sharp hospital-and-antiseptic smell even before they reached the emergency bay. Omar had worked scenes like that before, but this one had lodged itself in a different way because the victim’s face, the sound of their breathing, and the frantic pace of the handoff seemed to hold everything in a single unbearable moment. He later found that even the smallest reminders of victims — a face in distress, a body on a stretcher, the sight of wounds on someone in public — could pull him straight back into that night. When that happened, he would immediately try hard not to think about it, cutting off the image as soon as it surfaced and throwing himself into work or tasks to keep his mind occupied. At home he stayed busy with chores long after they needed doing, and at work he found reasons to stay moving rather than sit with anyone else’s distress.

The problem was that the more he forced the memory away, the more it seemed to return in fragments with the force of the original scene. Omar described that when it came back, it was not like remembering a story but like being dropped back into the ambulance and hospital bay all over again, with every sense lit up at once; the smell, the visual details, even the tension in his body felt completely real. There were parts of the event he simply could not account for, gaps he kept trying to fill but never could, and those missing pieces only deepened the terror each time he tried to review what had happened. He became convinced that something in him had broken permanently, that he had changed for the worse and could no longer rely on himself the way he once had. What haunted him most was the belief that he should have protected the victim better and that he had failed, a thought that made him scrutinize every decision afterward. That self-blame made him more alert to anything that resembled the original scene: visible injuries on others, reminders of victims, and the hospital smell all took on an immediate charge, and he would feel compelled to pull back, avoid going to work or study-related training sessions, and keep himself occupied so he would not have to face the images.

Over time, those habits began to narrow his life. Omar started arranging his days around not being confronted with the things that set him off, and even outside the hospital he chose seats based on how safe or protected he felt, usually with a wall at his back and a clear view of the room. If someone touched him unexpectedly, he reacted with alarm, and the reaction embarrassed him enough that he became even more vigilant about who stood behind him or approached too quickly. He noticed his concentration slipping during charting and routine conversations, partly because he was watching the room and partly because his mind kept drifting back to the same sensory flash of the call. The more he avoided, the less chance he had to settle the memory, and the less settled it became, the more often it intruded; the more often it intruded, the more certain he felt that he was damaged, unsafe, and responsible. That sense of being permanently altered fed the belief that he needed to stay busy and away from anything that might stir the event, yet the very act of skipping workdays, suppressing thoughts, and piling on extra tasks kept the trauma vivid and close, as if he were always bracing for the next reminder. Even now, a glimpse of injuries on a stranger or the antiseptic smell when he passed through the hospital corridors could set off the full sequence: alarm in his body, the surge of the memory, and the old conviction that he had failed and could not trust himself to do better.

He finally sought help after noticing that he was becoming increasingly withdrawn from his wife and more strained at work, where the job that once steadied him now felt like the most dangerous place to be. He was not asking because he wanted to stop caring; he was afraid that if this continued, the terror would keep taking over every part of his life, and he would end up proving to himself that he really was no longer the man he had been.
